Article Title: Tesla reports $1.53 billion in free cash flow amid one-fifth cut to 2026 spending forecast
Article Text:
Tesla cuts 2026 capex by one fifth

SpaceX merger puts Tesla's spending under scrutiny

Revenue beats estimates, but net income plunges 43%

FSD adoption and automotive margins improve

Tesla reported an unexpected $1.53 billion in free cash flow in the third quarter, beating Wall Street's expectations, as the electric vehicle maker spent less than anticipated on capital expenditure.However, a one-fifth cut to its 2026 spending forecast has raised questions about its investment plans for artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and autonomous driving. The company now expects capital expenditure of around $20 billion in 2026, down from its earlier forecast of more than $25 billion. Tesla did not specify which areas would see lower spending.In the quarter ended September 30, Tesla spent $4.7 billion on capital expenditure, double the amount spent a year earlier but well below the $7.5 billion analysts had expected on average, according to LSEG data.The lower spending helped Tesla report free cash flow of $1.53 billion, compared with market expectations of a cash outflow of $4.92 billion.Tesla's shares initially rose 2% in after-hours trading after the results, supported by positive free cash flow, higher gross margins and revenue that exceeded Wall Street expectations. However, the stock reversed direction to trade 2% lower. Shares have fallen around 14% this year."The free cash flow beat was a pleasant surprise, but when combined with the lower-than-expected capex, raises questions on the next step for the automaker," said Ryan Lee, senior vice president of product and strategy at Direxion, which offers exchange-traded funds tied to Tesla. "Lower capex suggests less of an 'all-in' approach to the AI arms race than one would expect from Elon."The results come as chief executive Elon Musk explores a potential combination of Tesla and SpaceX, his space venture. The unexpected cash generation could strengthen Tesla's financial position ahead of a possible deal, but lower investment in AI, robotaxis and humanoid robots could raise concerns about its ability to deliver on its growth ambitions.On Tuesday, Musk described a merger between the two companies as a "good idea" and said they had formed special committees to discuss the proposal. He declined to provide further details during Wednesday's conference call with analysts.A combination would bring together businesses central to Musk's long-term vision of an integrated technology and manufacturing group spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications and transportation on Earth and beyond.However, investors will want to see whether Tesla is investing enough to turn Musk's ambitions into commercial businesses, particularly as the robotaxi rollout has lagged behind his promises."The merger still faces a high bar, but tonight’s numbers make the financial logic harder to ignore," said Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com."The main takeaway is that Tesla's surprisingly positive cash flow quarter did not come from stronger profits, but from spending billions less than planned at a time when SpaceX is preparing to invest up to $40 billion in a single quarter."Tesla's financial performance presented a mixed picture. Revenue remained flat compared with a year earlier, despite the end of US tax credits that had supported sales in the previous year. Nevertheless, the figure exceeded Wall Street's expectations.Net income fell 43% during the quarter.Tesla said it had ended the quarter with its largest backlog of passenger vehicles in four years. Higher petrol prices have supported demand for electric vehicles, particularly in Europe.The company delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, putting it on track to increase annual deliveries for the first time in three years."Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It's exceeding our production by a significant margin," Musk said on the conference call with analysts. "In a nutshell, after many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we're now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth."Tesla also reported stronger adoption of its driver-assistance technology in North America. The FSD (supervised) attach rate exceeded three-quarters of new vehicle deliveries, an increase of nearly 20 percentage points from the second quarter, the company said.Automotive gross margin, excluding regulatory credits, reached 18.1% in the third quarter, above analysts' estimate of 16.7%, according to Visible Alpha data.Tesla's energy business has recently helped offset pressures on its automotive operations. The latter remain under scrutiny as competitors worldwide launch newer, often cheaper models. Tesla continues to rely heavily on its ageing Model 3 and Model Y.Despite the competitive pressures, Tesla aims to produce five million vehicles annually by around 2030, compared with an expected 2.5 million this year.
Article Summary: Tesla reports $1.53 billion in free cash flow, beating Wall Street's expectations. Company cuts 2026 capex forecast by one fifth to $20 billion, down from $25 billion. Results come as CEO Elon Musk explores a potential combination of Tesla and SpaceX.

Article Title: Rupee under pressure: Currency slips to 94.50 as oil rises, Dalal Street struggles in red
Article Text:
Rupee gives up some gains

NEW DELHI: Rupee weakened in early trade on Thursday, losing 12 paise to 94.50 against the US dollar as rising crude oil prices and a decline in the equity market weighed down the currency. A softer dollar and lower US treasury yields, however, helped limit the fall.The currency opened at 94.47 at the interbank foreign exchange market before slipping to 94.50. The decline came a day after the rupee had climbed 53 paise to close at 94.38 against the dollar on Wednesday.Forex analysts said the rupee was trading on a flat-to-lower note amid pressure from the domestic stock market and higher oil prices. The dollar’s weakness and easing US Treasury yields offered some support to the currency.Anuj Choudhary, research analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan, expects rupee to retain a slight positive bias."We expect the rupee to trade with a slight positive bias on IPO related foreign inflows and weakness in the dollar. Softening of US treasury yields and reports that Russia is ready for new peace talks may also support the rupee," he told PTI.Choudhary added that market participants would track the weekly unemployment claims data from the US for further direction.The dollar index, which tracks the US currency against a basket of six currencies, fell 0.21 per cent to 101.56. In contrast, Brent crude futures rose 1.58 per cent to $110.54 per barrel.Anindya Banerjee, head of commodity and currency research at Kotak NEO, said the rupee remained finely balanced within the 94-97 range."The RBI has bought itself time, the Jio IPO has added near-term dollar supply, and a US trade agreement could strengthen the structural inflow story. But if portfolio selling accelerates again or crude makes a decisive move towards $120, that balance will be tested," Banerjee added.The domestic equity market also remained under pressure during early trade. BSE Sensex dropped 642.51 points to 73,067.18, while NSE Nifty50 declined 241.35 points to 22,570.90.Despite the weakness in equities on Thursday morning, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) were net buyers in the previous session. They purchased equities worth Rs 1,022.32 crore on Wednesday, according to exchange data.
Article Summary: Rupee loses 12 paise to 94.50 against the US dollar in early trade on Thursday. Rising crude oil prices and a decline in the equity market weighed down the currency. A softer dollar and lower US treasury yields, however, helped limit the fall. The decline came a day after the rupee had climbed 53 paise against the dollar.

Article Title: France’s economic woes: Debt nears 122% of GDP, growth forecast at just 0.4%
Article Text:
France’s debt, taxes and borrowing costs rise as economic growth slows

France’s public debt nears 122% of GDP

Government spending accounts for 57.2% of GDP

France faces higher borrowing costs

France’s growth forecast falls to 0.4%

France is facing mounting pressure on two fronts: growing public anger over the cost of living and an economy struggling with high debt, taxes and weak growth. Student protests that began with school blockades have spread, turning violent, putting the spotlight on the country’s economic troubles and deepening political tensions.The rising cost of living is one of the concerns behind the demonstrations, which began largely peacefully but disrupted schools before escalating into wider unrest and pockets of violence involving young people on Saturday. The issue is not unique to France, but it comes at a difficult time for the country’s economy.France is also struggling to bring its public finances under control. Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING bank, said “France is not Greece”, referring to the financial crisis that shook the European Union in 2009. However, France has repeatedly failed to meet its targets for spending, economic growth and cost-cutting.With President Emmanuel Macron nearing the end of his nearly decade-long tenure, the state of the country’s finances is also expected to be a key issue in the race to succeed him next spring.France’s public debt stood at nearly 3.6 trillion euros (nearly $4.08 trillion) at the end of June, equivalent to 119% of its gross domestic product (GDP).The government has warned that the figure could rise further. Three weeks ago, it said the budget would again exceed European Union spending limits, with public debt expected to reach nearly 122% of GDP, setting a new record, AP reported.The growing debt leaves the government with difficult choices. It needs to reduce spending or raise taxes, which are already among the highest in Europe.Gilbert Cette, an economics professor at Neoma Business School in Paris, described the debt as “enormous”, saying, “France’s entire economic policy is constrained by such a sizable debt level.”Cette said France had shown “talent” in both increasing government spending and cutting taxes in recent years, making it harder to get public finances back on track.Brzeski also warned that France’s approach to economic reforms was affecting its credibility. Writing last week, he said, “Greece’s credibility was destroyed by false statistics; France’s is being eroded by false promises and the inability or unwillingness to start fiscal and structural reforms,”High government spending is another challenge for France. In 2025, public expenditure accounted for 57.2% of the country’s economic output, according to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency. The EU average was just under 50%.A large share of this spending goes towards healthcare, pensions and subsidies for businesses. With government expenditure already making up such a large part of the economy, reducing it further would require difficult decisions.France also has one of the highest tax burdens in the European Union. Tax revenue and social contributions accounted for 45.2% of GDP in 2024, putting the country a close second behind Denmark, according to Eurostat. The EU average was just over 40%.This leaves the government with limited room to raise taxes further to reduce the deficit. Cutting spending is another option, but it would mean making choices about areas that already account for a significant share of the economy.The cost of borrowing is adding to the pressure on France’s public finances. The yield on its 10-year government bond stood at 4.96% as of Tuesday.Higher bond yields mean the government has to pay more to borrow money. This can leave less room in the budget for other priorities, including pensions, education, healthcare, defence and social programmes.Germany, the European Union’s largest economy, faces lower borrowing costs. Its equivalent 10-year government bond, known as the Bund, had a yield of about 3.4%.The gap between French and German 10-year bond yields has widened, highlighting the difference in borrowing costs between the two countries. This adds to the challenges facing France as it tries to manage its debt and spending.France’s economic outlook remains weak. The International Monetary Fund has forecast growth of just 0.4% for the country this year, the lowest rate among developed economies.The forecast is well below the expected growth rates for both the global economy and advanced economies. Global output is projected to grow by 3.1% this year, while advanced economies are expected to expand by 2.1%.France’s projected growth is around one-third of Germany’s forecast rate and half of Italy’s. Japan, which has the second-lowest growth forecast among developed countries, is expected to grow by 0.7%.Slow growth makes it harder for France to manage its public finances while dealing with high debt, substantial government spending and an already heavy tax burden. Rising borrowing costs further add to the pressure.With the economy growing slowly and public finances under strain, France faces difficult choices over how to control its debt and spending. These economic challenges are unfolding alongside political divisions and protests over the cost of living, while the state of public finances is set to remain an important issue ahead of next spring’s presidential succession race.
Article Summary: France’s public debt stood at nearly 3.6 trillion euros (nearly $4.08 trillion) at the end of June, equivalent to 119% of its gross domestic product (GDP) The government has warned that the figure could rise further, with public debt expected to reach nearly 122% of GDP. High government spending is another challenge for France. In 2025, public expenditure accounted for 57.2% of the country's economic output, according to Eurostat.

Article Title: Sebi plans curbs on terminal misuse, graded compliance norms for stock market intermediaries
Article Text:
Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey

AI safeguards and digital market infrastructure

Pandey urges brokers to focus on investor risks

NEW DELHI: Market regulator Sebi is planning measures to prevent the misuse of brokers' trading terminals while also considering different compliance requirements for brokers based on their size, clients and use of technology.Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey announced the plans on Saturday at the 16th ANMI International Capital Market Convention in Mumbai. He also spoke about improving cybersecurity, testing artificial intelligence (AI) tools safely and boosting trading in corporate bonds."We are developing a framework to put in place safeguards to prevent misuse of trading terminals," Pandey said at the event organised by the Association of National Exchanges Members of India (ANMI).Under the proposed system, compliance rules would vary according to the size of a brokerage firm, its clients and its dependence on technology. Sebi also plans to bring inspection portals onto a single digital platform to make supervision faster and more consistent.Pandey urged market participants to treat cybersecurity as a business priority rather than an IT expense. He also called on them to test their systems and prepare for possible failures.Sebi is exploring an AI sandbox in which new tools can be tested safely, while providing innovators with regulatory clarity. The regulator is also finalising guidelines for the responsible use of AI, with provisions for accountability, data controls, kill switches and human oversight, in line with the International Organization of Securities Commissions' (IOSCO) toolkit."We are finalising the guidelines on the responsible use of AI. They will follow a tiered approach, with clear accountability, data controls, kill switches and human oversight, in line with IOSCO's toolkit," he added.The regulator's technology agenda also extends to the corporate debt market. A market-making framework is being developed to encourage secondary trading in corporate bonds, while the next phase of Demat 2.0 will involve tokenised corporate bonds trading in the secondary market.“In the next phase of Demat 2.0, tokenised corporate bonds will trade in the secondary market, bringing better liquidity, lower settlement risk, and faster access to funds,” he said.Sebi is separately reviewing short selling and securities lending and borrowing to improve liquidity and price discovery. Rules for depository participants are also being reworked to simplify compliance and strengthen defences against fraud.Turning to retail participation, Pandey said the next wave of growth in broking would come from towns and villages rather than big cities. Citing Sebi surveys indicating interest among Indians in investing in markets, he called on the industry to help investors make informed decisions and remain invested for longer.He urged brokers to look beyond completing know-your-customer (KYC) formalities and pay attention to whether the risks their clients take are in line with their financial resources."You are often the first to see when the risk they take outgrows their resources. So think of KYC as "Know Your Client's Needs." Make it an ongoing conversation, not a one-time form-filling exercise."Pandey said investors who understood the risks of their investments were better placed to make informed decisions and stay invested."A client who understands risk invests wisely and stays invested longer. That is good for the client, for you and for the market," he added.Outlining Sebi's broader priorities, Pandey said the regulator's roadmap centred on simpler rules, deeper markets, responsible technology and wider access.“Our roadmap has four parts: simpler rules, deeper markets, responsible technology, and wider access,” he reiterated.
Article Summary: Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey announced the plans on Saturday at the 16th ANMI International Capital Market Convention in Mumbai. He also spoke about improving cybersecurity, testing artificial intelligence (AI) tools safely and boosting trading in corporate bonds. Pandey urged market participants to treat cybersecurity as a business priority rather than an IT expense.

Article Title: US Fed expected to hold rates as inflation, energy costs weigh ahead of midterms
Article Text:
US Fed expected to hold interest rates steady despite persistent inflation (representative image)

Inflation pressures complicate Fed's rate decision

Former Fed official says economic data favour further hikes

Trump's criticism of Fed independence

The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged at its meeting next week, despite persistent inflation and market expectations of at least one more rate hike before the end of the year, according to analysts cited by news agency AFP.The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will meet over two days, with its interest rate decision scheduled for 2 pm local time (1800 GMT) on Wednesday.At its September meeting, the Fed raised its benchmark federal funds rate for the first time in three years, taking the target range to 3.75%-4%. The central bank has struggled to bring inflation down to its long-term target of 2%, which it has missed for more than five years.The decision comes just days before the November 3 US midterm elections, in which Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republican Party.The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, reached a pandemic-era peak of 7.2% in 2022 before a series of interest rate increases brought it down to around 2.2% by late 2024.However, inflation subsequently rose again amid Trump's economic policies, including tariffs that disrupted global trade and the US war with Iran. The PCE index reached a three-year high of 3.9% in May.Since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, global energy prices have surged, with retaliatory actions by Tehran sharply restricting oil and gas supplies through the Gulf. Higher energy costs have also begun feeding into the prices of other goods and services, putting affordability at the forefront of concerns ahead of the midterm elections.The Fed faces the challenge of controlling inflation while supporting the labour market. Higher interest rates increase borrowing costs, potentially slowing economic activity and curbing price pressures, but they can also weigh on employment.The US economy has also been dealing with weakening consumer confidence and signs of stress in an otherwise resilient jobs market. The latest consumer confidence survey from the Conference Board was expected to show a further decline in October after confidence fell in September to its lowest level in more than a decade.Loretta Mester, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, told AFP that the timing of the meeting ahead of the elections would not influence policymakers' decision."The Fed doesn't take into account any kind of political issues in that FOMC room," she said. "It really is based on the economics."Mester argued that economic conditions supported further monetary tightening, pointing to a stable labour market and inflation remaining above the central bank's target."The data that's come in continue to show a stable labor market and continue to show inflation above target," she said, adding that there was no evidence of inflation moving towards the target."The economics would suggest then you need to continue raising rates."However, Mester said most policymakers appeared reluctant to move too quickly. She expected the Fed could hold rates steady in October and consider another increase at its next meeting in early December.Wendy Edelberg, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, also said that central bankers would prefer to avoid becoming part of the political debate ahead of the elections."It's unhelpful for everyone if the Fed gets wrapped up in all the political discourse right before an election," she said.Edelberg added that raising rates in December rather than October would have limited economic implications.She viewed a possible delay less as a concession to Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower interest rates, and more as a way for the Fed to avoid becoming a target of political criticism.Trump has repeatedly criticised the Federal Reserve over interest rates, which he considers too high. However, he has so far refrained from directing similar criticism at Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed to succeed Jerome Powell as Fed chair.Since returning to power last year, Trump has mounted an unprecedented challenge to the central bank's independence. His administration launched a criminal investigation into Powell and attempted to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook.The investigation into Powell was dropped to smooth the way for Warsh's confirmation by the Senate, while the legal battle over Cook's removal continued despite a Supreme Court decision nullifying an earlier attempt to dismiss her.Last week, Cook declined to attend a hearing in a White House investigation into mortgage fraud allegations, which she denies.Meanwhile, the Fed's rate decision will come during a busy week for US economic data.Investors and policymakers were also awaiting updates on inflation, consumer confidence and third-quarter economic growth, alongside earnings reports from major companies.
Article Summary: US Federal Reserve is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged at its meeting next week. The central bank has struggled to bring inflation down to its long-term target of 2%. The decision comes just days before the November 3 US midterm elections, in which Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both chambers of Congress.
